_comment: Registry for the semantic lifting loop (DECOMP-LIFT-PILOT-001, extended by
One entry per reconstructed translation unit. Function boundaries are never
restated by hand: GBARam's come from config/compiler_probes.json, and the
ByteCodeInterpreter's are re-derived from the ROM on every run and checked
against the recorded extents. See docs/LIFT_LOOP.md.
`compiler` describes the MODERN toolchain configuration only. It is not a
claim about the original compiler, and no result from it may be reported as
`semantic_minimum_checks` is per target on purpose. One global number would
either wave through a truncated run of a small self-check or fail a
`host_build_bits` selects the host toolchain width. A reconstruction that
holds pointers in u32 fields models a 32-bit machine: built 64-bit, the high
half of every stored address is lost and the first dereference through one
faults. This is a property of the machine model, not something to widen away.

targets.name: GBARam allocator
targets.role: small-block heap allocator: initialise, unlink, insert, merge, allocate, free, total free
targets.notes: the first lifted family. Chosen because it is the only region in the ROM map whose boundaries are independently established: eight functions recovered by chain-walk recursive descent, every path terminating, zero gaps, zero undecodable bytes, and one shared 4-word literal pool that proves it was a single translation unit. The surviving original build command names it directly: tcpp -S -c -cpu ARM7TDMI -O1 src/GBARam.c.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter dispatch loop
targets.role: script engine: the bytecode dispatch loop, the dialog entry point that calls it, and one untitled helper sharing the same literal pool
targets.notes: the first real engine subsystem. The ROM preserves the original source path T:\Source\ByteCodeInterpreter\ByteCodeInterpreter.cpp as ASCII at 0x08004160, referenced by the assertion at 0x080040F4. The unit is three functions because they share ONE 8-byte literal pool at 0x08004158, which is what establishes a single compilation unit. The pool is NOT adjacent to the code: two alignment bytes separate them and 86 bytes of unrelated code sit between. The dispatch table at 0x080554C0 has 31 entries, bounded by the UTF-16 assertion string at 0x0805553C. The 31 handler targets and the native table are deliberately NOT decompiled here; the native table is 266 entries, measured and proved by DECOMP-LIFT-SCRIPT-HANDLER-001 (a prior claim of 283 is refuted).

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter primary slot 2
targets.role: the handler that reaches the native dispatch table: consumes a one-byte native index and selects native[index]
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 2, entry 0x08003CBE, 22 bytes and 10 instructions. A separate translation unit from the interpreter: separate code and a separate literal pool at 0x08003F40, which four other primary handlers (slots 21-24) also load from. It is reached ONLY through the primary dispatch table, so a direct-call census correctly returns nothing. Handler 2 never writes r0, so the context is passed to the native routine unchanged; 10 of 12 sampled native routines read r0 before writing it, and none read r2, so r0 is the argument and the table base left in r2 is incidental. The native table has 266 entries, bounded below by the one-byte index (256 values must all be in range) and above by the primary table base at 0x080554C0; a prior 283-entry claim reaches 0x08055504, inside the primary table, and is refuted. No native routine is reconstructed and no native index is named.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter primary slot 1 (operand reader)
targets.role: reads a variable-length sign-magnitude operand from the cursor and pushes it onto the context's value stack
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 1, entry 0x08003C8A, 52 bytes and 26 instructions. A LEAF: no calls and NO literal pool, so it needed no helper and no pool stubbing. Its only entry is primary table word 0x08003C8B, and no direct BL site targets it. The encoding read off the instructions: big-endian base-128 groups, bit 7 of each byte continues the sequence, bit 0 of the accumulator is the sign and the rest is the magnitude, extracted with an arithmetic shift. 1 byte reaches -63, 2 -8191, 3 -1048575, 4 -134217727. There is NO length limit and no validation: the only exit is a byte with bit 7 clear. The arithmetic shift makes the sign invert once accumulator bit 31 is set, so the maximal five-group sequence 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F decodes to +1 rather than -2147483647; that is recorded as the code's actual behaviour and reproduced exactly, not corrected. The value is pushed at context+0x00 (a counter) and context+4+4*index, which proves the field the interpreter zeroes at 0x0800405C is a stack counter. 'sm7' is NOT a ROM string: it is a project nickname recorded as a candidate alias only.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter value-stack consumer (primary slot 7)
targets.role: the first consumer of the value stack: pops the top value, adds it to the new top in place, and leaves the sum in the lower slot
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 7, entry 0x08003D3E, 20 bytes and 10 instructions. The smallest function in the image holding the value-stack pop idiom, and a leaf with no calls and no literal pool. 84 functions in the VM surface contain the idiom (111 pops total; 69 native, 15 primary), so this is one of a family, but only this one is lifted. It consumes two values and produces one, a net counter delta of -1, and the result is written to the LOWER operand slot values[count-2] while the upper slot is abandoned rather than cleared. The counter is written back BEFORE the operand reads, which the underflow proves. There is NO underflow check: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, the slot address becomes context-4, and the handler decrements the word immediately BELOW the context object while touching no value slot; successive underflows walk the base four bytes further down each time. That is recorded as actual behaviour and reproduced exactly, including the 32-bit address wrap the modelling depends on. The operand order values[count-2] <op> values[count-1] is not observable in this handler because addition is commutative; it is established by the sibling at primary slot 8 (0x08003D52), which shares the first eight instructions and performs `subs r1, r2, r1`. Slots 8 and 9 are NOT lifted. No opcode table is reconstructed and no opcode index is named.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter value-stack arithmetic (primary slots 8 and 9)
targets.role: the rest of the value-stack arithmetic family: slot 8 subtracts the top from the deeper value, slot 9 multiplies them
targets.notes: primary dispatch slots 8 (0x08003D52) and 9 (0x08003D66), 20 bytes and 10 instructions each, mutually adjacent and adjacent to slot 7 which is lifted separately so its report stays reproducible. Both are leaves: no calls and no literal pool. The three tile 0x08003D3E..0x08003D7A and differ in exactly one instruction - `adds r1, r2, r1`, `subs r1, r2, r1`, `muls r2, r1, r2`. Slot 8 is the member that proves the operand order for the whole family, because addition and multiplication are commutative: `subs r1, r2, r1` computes r2 - r1, r2 holds the lower slot and r1 the top, so the shared contract is `deeper = FIRST source, top = SECOND source`. Note slot 9's combining instruction writes r2 rather than r1, so its store is `str r2,[r0]` where the others store r1; the result register differs but the slot written and the contract do not. All three are plain 32-bit operations with no saturation and no overflow branch, so `muls` keeps only the low half of a 64-bit product. There is NO underflow check in any member: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF and the arithmetic runs against the word immediately below the context object - slot 8 INCREMENTS it (deeper - 0xFFFFFFFF = deeper + 1) and slot 9 replaces it with its own negation (0xFFFFFFFF * deeper = -deeper) - while no value slot is touched, and successive underflows walk four bytes further down. Reproduced exactly, with no guard added. No opcode table is reconstructed and no opcode index is given a name beyond the operation its own instruction performs.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter surviving-value consumer (native entry 29)
targets.role: pop one value and pass it to a call, with a global field as the other argument
targets.notes: native dispatch entry 29, code address 0x080007E6, 24 bytes and 11 instructions, one terminator at 0x080007FC. A mechanical scan of both proven dispatch tables found 52 functions that pop a stack value and do NOT write a result back into the slot; this is the smallest of them, with one pop, one call, one literal and no branches. It is the first routine in the target chain that turns a surviving stack value into an actual use: it decrements the counter, reads values[count-1], and passes that value as the SECOND argument (r1) to sub_08004380, with the FIRST argument (r0) being the +0x14 field of the object at the routine's only literal 0x08054FBC. Nothing is written back to the stack, so the consumed slot keeps its old value and no result replaces it, which is what distinguishes it from the arithmetic family. Ordering is proven by the self-check reading the counter from inside the callee: the counter store precedes the value read, which precedes the call. UNDERFLOW IS HARMLESS TO MEMORY here, unlike the arithmetic family: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, the base becomes context-4, and [slot+4] is therefore context itself, so the value passed on underflow is the brand-new counter 0xFFFFFFFF; because the routine has no store to the slot, nothing below the context is read or written. A second underflow walks the base down and reads pre[3] instead. No guard was added. The callee is declared, not reconstructed, and no meaning is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter VM value effect (sub_08004380)
targets.role: set one bit of a byte array inside an object, from the value the VM popped
targets.notes: sub_08004380, 22 bytes and 11 instructions, one terminator at 0x08004394, no branches, NO calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF, so the effect is established by this routine alone and no helper had to be followed. Its argument contract is already proven from its caller: native dispatch entry 29 passes r0 = *(0x08054FBC + 0x14) and r1 = values[count-1] popped from the VM stack. THE CONCRETE EFFECT: it sets bit (value & 7) of the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55, preserving the other seven bits. The two shifts are the standard bit-array split - `asrs r2, r1, #3` selects the byte, `lsls r3, r1, #0x1d` then `lsrs r3, r3, #0x1d` isolates the low three bits to select the bit within it - and `orrs` plus `strb` make it a read-modify-write. THE BYTE-INDEX SHIFT IS ARITHMETIC, which matters: a value with bit 31 set gives a negative byte index and the write lands BEFORE the base. 0xFFFFFFFF maps to base + 0x54 bit 7, one byte before its unsigned position, and 0x80000000 maps to base + 0xF0000055, nowhere near the logical-shift answer of base + 0x10000055. THE RECONSTRUCTION MODELS THE ARITHMETIC SHIFT EXPLICITLY because C's right shift of a negative signed value is implementation-defined. THERE IS NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check: no compare against a size and no conditional branch exists anywhere in the routine, so every value selects a byte and that byte is written, however far outside the object it lies. No guard was added. UNKNOWN: what the bit MEANS, how large the byte array is, and what reads the bit afterwards. No name is assigned to the object, the array or the bit, and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter bit-array reader (sub_08004364)
targets.role: test one bit of the byte array the effect routine writes, and return 0 or 1
targets.notes: sub_08004364, 28 bytes and 14 instructions, two terminators at 0x0800437A and 0x0800437E, no calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF sitting immediately before the setter sub_08004380, with the clearer sub_08004396 immediately after it, so the three tile 0x08004364..0x080043AC as one bit-array accessor trio. THE INDEX SPLIT IS IDENTICAL TO THE SETTER'S: `asrs r2, r1, #3` selects the byte and the `lsls r2, r1, #0x1d` / `lsrs r2, r2, #0x1d` pair isolates the low three bits, so it reads the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55, the same byte the setter writes. The byte-index shift is ARITHMETIC, so a value with bit 31 set reads BEFORE the base, exactly as the setter writes. IT TESTS THE BIT FOR SET: `ands` masks the byte with 1 << (value & 7) and the routine branches on whether the result is zero. THE RETURN VALUE IS A NORMALISED BOOLEAN, 0 or 1, not the masked byte, so a caller cannot see which bit was masked. IT WRITES NOTHING: there is no store anywhere in the routine, which is what makes it a reader rather than the setter or the clearer. There is NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check. THE FIRST OBSERVABLE CONSEQUENCE: three call sites consume the boolean, and all three treat the bit as a predicate - at 0x080007C4 the boolean is materialised into a word slot by `str r0, [r4]`; at 0x080007DA the INVERTED boolean is materialised by `movs r1,#1 ; subs r0, r1, r0 ; str r0, [r4]`; and at 0x080032EE the boolean gates setting a bit in a packed local word (`cmp r0,#0 ; beq ; movs r0,#1 ; lsls r0,r4 ; orrs r6,r0`), a gather loop copying set bits out of the array. So the bit's first concrete consequence is that it becomes a 0/1 value in an engine slot, and one caller deliberately inverts it. WHAT THE BIT MEANS IS STILL UNKNOWN: no semantic name is assigned to the flag, the array or the object, the array's size is unknown, and what reads the materialised word afterwards is not followed. Nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter boolean materialisation (sub_080007B6, sub_080007CC)
targets.role: replace the stack top with the flag bit, and with its inverse
targets.notes: sub_080007B6 (22 bytes, 10 instructions) and sub_080007CC (26 bytes, 12 instructions), adjacent, one terminator each at 0x080007CA and 0x080007E4, one call each to the already-lifted reader sub_08004364, and one shared literal at 0x080008D8. THE DESTINATION IS THE SAME AT BOTH SITES, and it is derived rather than assumed: each computes its address as `context + count*4` from the counter at context+0x00 (`ldr r1,[r0] ; lsls r1,r1,#2 ; adds r4,r1,r0`), and the value stack holds values[i] at context + 4 + 4*i, so context + count*4 is context + 4 + 4*(count-1), which is values[count-1], THE TOP OF THE STACK. Both routines therefore REPLACE THE STACK TOP IN PLACE. This is NOT a pop: neither stores to context+0x00, so the COUNTER IS UNCHANGED, and it is not a separate word either. The two differ only in what they store: the first stores the flag (0 or 1), the second stores 1 - flag, so for a boolean input the second is the exact inverse of the first. Both return the value they stored in r0, and neither reads r1. THE STACK IS NOT CHECKED FOR BEING EMPTY: with a counter of zero the computed address is context + 0, so the word read is the COUNTER itself and the store REPLACES THE COUNTER with the flag, leaving the count at 0 or 1. No guard was added. THE FIRST CONCRETE CONSEQUENCE, proven through the already-lifted consumer sub_080007E6 which begins immediately after these two at 0x080007E6: it pops values[count-1] and passes it to sub_08004380, which sets bit (value & 7) of the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55. With a materialised boolean the index is 0 or 1, so THE BOOLEAN SELECTS WHICH BIT IS SET in the first byte of the flag array - bit 0 when the tested flag was clear, bit 1 when it was set. The boolean is therefore used as a BIT INDEX by the first consumer downstream of it, not as a truth value. UNKNOWN: what either bit means, whether callers rely on the counter being untouched, and what reads the array afterwards. No semantic name is assigned, and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter bit-array clearer (sub_08004396)
targets.role: clear one bit of the byte array with a read-modify-write
targets.notes: sub_08004396, 22 bytes and 11 instructions, one terminator at 0x080043AA, no calls and NO literal pool. It is the third and last member of the bit-array accessor trio, sitting immediately after the setter at 0x08004380, so the reader, the setter and this clearer tile 0x08004364..0x080043AC. DERIVED ON ITS OWN EVIDENCE, not by assuming it mirrors the setter: the differing instruction is `bics`, which computes byte & ~(1 << (value & 7)) - a bit CLEAR - where the setter uses `orrs`. The index split is the same as the other two: `asrs #3` selects the byte, the `lsls`/`lsrs #0x1d` pair isolates the low three bits, and the byte is at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55. The byte-index shift is ARITHMETIC, so a value with bit 31 set clears BEFORE the base. It is a READ-MODIFY-WRITE: `ldrb` reads, `bics` clears, `strb` writes back, so the other seven bits of that byte survive; exactly one byte is modified. There is NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check. THE RETURN VALUE IS NOT DEFINED: the routine ends with `bx lr` with r0 still holding the computed field address, not a status or a boolean, so the reconstruction returns void rather than inventing a result. Clearing an already-clear bit is a no-op, and clearing the same bit twice equals clearing it once; both are asserted. UNKNOWN: what the bit means, and how large the array is. No semantic name is assigned and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter flag-array gather loop (sub_080032C2)
targets.role: gather a run of flag bits into a mask and push it back onto the VM stack
targets.notes: sub_080032C2, 78 bytes and 38 instructions, one terminator at 0x0800330E, one call to the already-lifted reader sub_08004364, and one literal 0x08054FBC. No BL caller targets it anywhere in the image, so it is reached by VM dispatch: it is the function the flagread report recorded as the reader's third call site 0x080032EE. IT IS A TWO-INTO-ONE REDUCTION OVER THE FLAG ARRAY rather than over its two operands: it POPS a BOUND from the top and a BIT OFFSET from beneath it, then for n = 0 .. bound-1 tests the array bit at `offset + n` and sets bit n of an accumulator when that flag is set, finally PUSHING the mask as a new stack value. Net counter movement is -1, two consumed and one produced, so it leaves a result on the VM stack rather than escaping the VM. THE VALUE PASSED TO THE READER IS `offset + n`, NOT `n` (`adds r1, r0, r4`), which is the detail that fixes the meaning: the second operand is a BIT NUMBER in the array, not a byte index and not a pointer, and successive iterations test successive BITS from that offset. LOOP BOUNDS: the loop runs while n < bound with n starting at 0, so a positive bound gathers exactly that many bits; a bound of zero or LESS is skipped entirely by the `ble`, which compares the bound as signed, producing a mask of 0 with no call to the reader at all; there is NO upper clamp, and the shift amount is the RUNTIME loop index, so the ARCHITECTURAL rule applies: ARM7TDMI register-controlled LSL yields ZERO at an amount of 32 or more, so every iteration at n >= 32 ORs in nothing and the mask can never carry a bit above 31 whatever the bound is. AN EARLIER REVISION OF THIS ENTRY AND REPORT CLAIMED THE AMOUNT WAS TAKEN MODULO 32; THAT IS NOT THE ARM7TDMI RULE AND WAS CORRECTED BY DECOMP-FLAGSTATE-SHIFT-FIX-001. THE RESULTING MASK: bit n is the flag array bit at (offset + n), so the mask is the packed run of flags from the caller's offset. Its DESTINATION is the VM stack itself - the routine increments the counter and stores the mask at values[count] - so the mask becomes the new stack top, to be consumed by whatever pops it next, which is as far as this ticket follows it. NO BOUNDS CHECK, NO NULL CHECK, AND NO SIZE KNOWLEDGE: neither the offset nor the bound is compared against any size, and the array size is not reachable from this routine at all. ARRAY EXTENT: the proven LOWER bound is one byte, eight bits, because the trio addresses one byte at base + 0x55 and the boolean transforms only ever produce indices 0 and 1; no static UPPER bound is derivable from code evidence, because no instruction compares an index against a size and the gather loop's offset and bound are runtime values. No guard was added. UNKNOWN: what the gathered mask means, how large the array is, and what pops the mask.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter flag-mask application (sub_08003310)
targets.role: apply a mask to a run of flag bits: set where a bit is 1, clear where it is 0
targets.notes: sub_08003310, 86 bytes and 41 instructions, one terminator at 0x08003364, native dispatch entry 187, calls the already-lifted setter sub_08004380 and clearer sub_08004396, one literal 0x08054FBC. It begins IMMEDIATELY WHERE THE GATHER ENDS at 0x08003310, and it is the first consumer of the mask that gather pushes. STACK BEHAVIOUR: it POPPED three values in order - the MASK from the stack top, then the WIDTH, then the BIT OFFSET - and pushes NOTHING, so the counter moves by exactly -3 and the mask is never written back to the stack. MASK INTERPRETATION: it is not merely tested or stored. The routine applies it per bit: for i = 0..width-1 it SETS the flag at (offset + i) when mask bit i is 1 and CLEARS it when that bit is 0, so EACH BIT OF THE MASK BECOMES THE STATE OF THE CORRESPONDING FLAG. That makes it the exact counterpart of the gather that produced it, and it is the first concrete engine consequence of the gathered mask. The bit under test is always mask bit 0, because `lsls r2, r4, #0x1f` moves it into bit 31 for the `beq` and `asrs r4, r4, #1` then brings the next bit down. TWO CLAMPS, BOTH SIGNED: a mask that is negative when read as signed is replaced by 0 entirely, and a mask where (1 << width) is not greater is truncated to (1 << width) - 1. ORDERING: all three pops complete before the first flag is touched, and the offset is added to the loop index immediately before each call. WIDTH 32 IS A REAL EDGE CASE, reproduced rather than corrected: ARM LSL by a register yields ZERO for an amount of 32 or more, so at a width of 32 the width clamp computes 0 - 1 = 0xFFFFFFFF EVEN FOR A MASK OF 0, and `asrs` keeps it all ones, so all 32 flags are SET. A width of zero or less is skipped entirely by the `ble`, though the three values are still consumed. THE THUMB SHIFT IS MODELLED EXPLICITLY rather than left to C, because `1u << 32` is undefined in C and MSVC masks the amount to five bits and yields 1, which is the opposite of the machine. NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check. UNKNOWN: what the flags mean, and how large the array is. No semantic name is assigned, and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter native slot 178 (sub_08003030)
targets.role: pop three VM values and drive an engine object with the result
targets.notes: Native dispatch slot 178, 0x08003030, 64 bytes and 30 instructions, one terminator at 0x0800306E, two calls, one literal 0x08054FBC. IDENTITY IS CROSS-VALIDATED STATIC AND RUNTIME: the native table at 0x08055098 holds 0x08003031 at slot 178 (table address 0x08055360), whose Thumb bit masks off to 0x08003030, which is exactly the address an independent 2026 runtime capture recorded for slot 178; the two agree, and exactly ONE table entry points here. THE RUNTIME CAPTURE IS USED ONLY AS IDENTITY EVIDENCE and no semantic claim rests on it. THE ENTRY CONTRACT: r0 is the interpreter context and is used as the base of the value stack, reading the counter at +0x00 and the values at +4+4*i; r1 IS NEVER READ, because the first instruction is `ldr r1,[r0]` which overwrites it, so no argument meaning is assigned to it despite the dispatcher leaving the routine's own address there incidentally. STACK BEHAVIOUR: it POPS THREE values and PUSHES NOTHING, so the counter moves by exactly -3, and it reads them top-first as values[count-1], values[count-2], values[count-3]. It builds a TWO-ELEMENT ARRAY ON ITS OWN FRAME rather than on the VM stack: local[1] takes values[count-1] and local[0] takes values[count-2], so the pair is handed to the callee DEEPEST-OF-THE-TWO FIRST, which is the reverse of VM stack order. No value slot is written, so the consumed slots are abandoned rather than cleared. THERE IS NO STACK GUARD: no comparison of the counter against zero or three exists, so a counter below three wraps and the reads walk below the context object; that is reproduced rather than guarded, and the self-check pins it, including that POP 2's `+1` wraps onto the counter itself and POP 3 lands on the word immediately below the context. THE FIRST CONCRETE NON-STACK EFFECT: the handler makes TWO calls and returns nothing to the VM - `result = sub_0802BFBC(values[count-3], { values[count-2], values[count-1] })` and then `sub_0801191A(*(0x08054FBC + 0x18), result)`. The second call is the observable engine effect, handing the first call's result to an engine routine together with the object named by the table word at 0x08054FBC + 0x18, which is the IWRAM address 0x03001C4C. Both callees are DECLARED, not reconstructed, and are bound at their original addresses, so nothing was lifted beyond this handler. UNKNOWN: what sub_0802BFCC computes, what sub_0801191A does with the object and the result, and what the object at 0x03001C4C is. No semantic name is assigned and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter object append (sub_0801191A)
targets.role: append a value to the array carried by the object at 0x03001C4C
targets.notes: sub_0801191A, 18 bytes and 9 instructions, one terminator at 0x0801192A, NO calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF, so the effect is established by this routine alone. THE CONCRETE EFFECT: it APPENDS the incoming value at index `count` of an array carried by the object, then increments that count. The object holds a 32-bit COUNT at +0x04 and an array of 32-bit values beginning at +0x08, so `sub_0801191A(object, value)` performs `((u32*)object)[1] += 1` and `*(u32*)(object + 8 + 4*count) = value`, where count is the value READ BEFORE the increment, so element `count` is written and not element `count+1`. OBJECT-RELATIVE ACCESSES, ALL OF THEM: +0x04 is read and then written 32-bit as the count; +0x08 + 4*count is written 32-bit as the appended element; and +0x00 IS NOT TOUCHED at all, neither read nor written. There is no other access in the routine. ORDER: the count is loaded first, stored back incremented second, and only then is the element written; both complete before the routine returns and nothing interrupts them. THERE IS NO CAPACITY CHECK: nothing compares the count against a limit and no capacity is reachable from this routine, so a large count writes far past any sane array end - the machine's behaviour, reproduced rather than guarded. THE RETURN VALUE IS NOT DEFINED: the routine ends with `bx lr` with r0 holding the address of the element it just wrote, not a status and not a boolean, so the reconstruction returns void rather than inventing a result. THE INCOMING CONTRACT, re-proven from the caller: native dispatch slot 178 at 0x08003030 calls this with r0 = *(0x08054FBC + 0x18), which the static layout resolves to the IWRAM object 0x03001C4C, and r1 = the value returned by sub_0802BFBC. THE FIRST CONCRETE EFFECT OF THE WHOLE CHAIN: slot 178 pops three VM values, computes one from them, and hands it here, where it is APPENDED to the object's array. So the object is a growable-by-write collection rather than a scalar and the handler is a producer for it. This object is the most heavily referenced entry in the static pointer table, so its count-and-array shape is recorded for reuse. UNKNOWN: what the object is, what its +0x00 field means, what the appended values are used for, who reads them, and whether a capacity limit exists elsewhere. No semantic name is assigned to the object, the array or the count, and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter collection reader (sub_08011C70)
targets.role: search the collection by virtual dispatch over its elements
targets.notes: sub_08011C70, 88 bytes and 44 instructions, one terminator at 0x08011CC8. It is called WITH the collection object in r0, and apart from the virtual call it makes it is a leaf. THE CONCRETE EFFECT: a SEARCH performed by VIRTUAL DISPATCH. For each element from the TOP of the collection DOWNWARD it dereferences the element, takes the method at offset +0x24 of the table the element's first word points at, calls it with the two incoming arguments unchanged, and RETURNS THE FIRST NON-ZERO RESULT IMMEDIATELY. If nothing matches it returns 0. THE COLLECTION LAYOUT, PROVEN A THIRD TIME AND NOW FROM DIFFERENT INSTRUCTIONS: count at collection + 0x04, elements from collection + 0x08, each element a 32-BIT POINTER to a virtual object whose FIRST WORD is a table pointer. TRAVERSAL: BACKWARD, from count-1 down to 0, so the MOST RECENTLY APPENDED element is tested FIRST; the index is decremented before the loop and the loop continues on `bpl`. COUNT 0: the index goes to -1 and the `bmi` skips the loop entirely, so an empty collection causes NO call at all. THE COUNT IS READ ONLY; there is no store to +0x04 anywhere. CAPACITY EVIDENCE, FOUND HERE AND NOT INFERRED: the routine searches a SECOND collection of the SAME SHAPE at object + 0x408, whose count is at object + 0x40C and whose elements begin at object + 0x410, because it adds 0x40C to the object base and then reads the count from that address. The object therefore carries TWO collections 0x408 bytes apart. +0x00 IS NOT TOUCHED by this reader. THE VIRTUAL CALL: the original reaches the method through the `bx r3` thunk at 0x08046AA6, a trampoline the original toolchain emitted for an indirect call; the reconstruction expresses the same operation as a plain call through a function pointer, which is what the trampoline achieves, so no external symbol is introduced. NO BOUNDS CHECK on the count and no null check on an element, and none was added. UNKNOWN: what the collection holds, what the element type or the method is, how large either collection may grow, and what +0x00 is. No semantic name is assigned and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter second-collection writer (sub_080119BC)
targets.role: keyed replace in the first collection, else remove the key from the second and append to the first
targets.notes: sub_080119BC, the routine that reaches the SECOND collection as a writer. THE WRITE CONTRACT: it scans the FIRST collection FORWARD from index 0 comparing each element against the KEY (second argument). If the key is found, it REPLACES that element with the value and does NOT touch any count. If the key is absent from the first collection it scans the SECOND collection the same way at object + 0x40C, and when the key is found there it REMOVES it through sub_0804FE54(object + 0x40C, index), then APPENDS the value to the FIRST collection, incrementing only the first collection's count. So it is a keyed MOVE ACROSS THE TWO COLLECTIONS. THE SECOND COLLECTION IS A WRITER TARGET ONLY THROUGH THAT REMOVAL: nothing here appends to it and nothing here increments its count. THE SECOND COLLECTION IS REACHED BY A COMPUTED BASE, NOT A DISPLACEMENT: the routine adds 0x40C to the object base once and works through that register afterwards, which is why an image-wide search for stores at a displacement near 0x40C finds NOTHING. That also explains why the count it reads is at object + 0x40C and the elements at object + 0x410 + 4*i, the shape the reader sub_08011C70 proved. ORDER: both scans run FORWARD, so the FIRST element equal to the key wins, the OPPOSITE direction from the reader's backward search. The value is stored VERBATIM. NO CAPACITY CHECK and no bounds check. +0x00 IS NOT TOUCHED. COMPARISON WITH sub_0801191A, and this is measured rather than inferred from their adjacency: they are NOT structurally equivalent at different offsets. sub_0801191A is a GENERIC append that takes any collection base, and its callers pass many different bases including *(r5+4), *(r5) and *(r7+0xc), so it is not tied to this object or to either of its collections. sub_080119BC hardcodes the 0x40C offset and knows about both of this object's collections. They are two members of ONE API FAMILY with DIFFERENT roles: a generic append, and an object-specific keyed move. UNKNOWN: what the elements mean, what sub_0804FE54 does beyond removing an entry and whether it compacts, and CRUCIALLY WHAT APPENDS TO THE SECOND COLLECTION - this routine only removes from it, so the second collection's INSERTION path is still unfound. The object's +0x00 field is untouched here. No semantic name is assigned and nothing is imported from another title. CORRECTION (DECOMP-LIFT-COLLECTION-INSERT2-001): an earlier revision of this note said the removal targeted object + 0x408. That was WRONG. The helper receives a pointer to the COUNT SLOT, not the collection base: sub_08011732 passes object + 4 for the first collection whose base is object + 0, so the same convention means this routine passes object + 0x40C, the second collection's count slot.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter second-collection insertion (sub_08011732)
targets.role: append a migrated element to the second collection
targets.notes: sub_08011732, 216 bytes and 97 instructions, one terminator at 0x08011808. THE INSERTION IS AT 0x0801177E..0x0801178A and reads `slot = second.count; second.count = slot + 1; second.elements[slot] = element`, using the OLD count as the index. HOW IT IS REACHED: the routine walks the FIRST collection BACKWARD from count-1 to 0 and asks each element's virtual method at table+0x18, passing a pass counter. A verdict of 1 makes it call table+0x04 and REMOVE the element from the first collection. A verdict of 2 makes it call table+0x1C, APPEND the element to the SECOND collection and REMOVE it from the first. Any other verdict leaves the element alone. So the second collection is filled by a VERDICT-DRIVEN MIGRATION out of the first, and the element is MOVED rather than copied: it exists in exactly one of the two collections afterwards. THE SECOND COLLECTION IS REACHED BY A COMPUTED BASE: the 0x40C literal is loaded into a register and added, so a displacement search finds nothing, exactly as in sub_080119BC. THIS IS THE INVERSE OF sub_080119BC, which moves an element from the second collection to the first when a key is found; together they are the two directions of one migration. ORDER: the inner loop runs BACKWARD, the same direction as the reader sub_08011C70 and the opposite of sub_080119BC's forward keyed scan. NO DUPLICATE CHECK: the element is appended at the tail whether or not an equal element is already in the second collection, so duplicate prevention is NOT a property of this path. NO CAPACITY CHECK and no bounds check on the second count. A THIRD COLLECTION EXISTS AT object + 0x208: the routine walks it calling table+0x14 on each element and then SETS ITS COUNT TO ZERO, so that collection is FLUSHED rather than migrated. THE REMOVAL HELPER TAKES THE COUNT SLOT, NOT THE COLLECTION BASE, which this routine proves by passing object + 4 for the first collection; the same convention means the call in sub_080119BC is sub_0804FE54(object + 0x40C, index) and an earlier note of ours saying object + 0x408 is corrected here. +0x00 IS NOT TOUCHED. UNKNOWN: what the elements are, what verdicts 1 and 2 mean beyond their effect, what sub_080116FC/sub_080115B0/sub_0803DA62 and the global at 0x08072824 do, and what appends to the third collection. No semantic name is assigned and nothing is imported from another title.
